info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 7.1: Rendering by Hand: Display Decisions, HTML, and CSS.

name.text: 01 Question: Your Edition So Far, and Why Nobody Can Read It Yet

questiontext.text: Your file transcription_normalized.xml is valid TEI. Why is it not yet a publication?

generalfeedback.text: A valid TEI file is a complete record of your document but not yet a publication; rendering is the step that turns it into something a reader can use.

answer.text: Its words are buried in markup that machines and editors can read but an ordinary reader cannot; it still has to be rendered.

feedback.text: Correct. A TEI file is a precise record, not a reader-friendly page. Rendering turns it into something a reader can use.

answer.text: It is missing the transcription, which is only added at the publication stage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The transcription is already in the file; you built it in Weeks 4 to 6.

answer.text: Valid TEI files are encrypted and must be unlocked before anyone can open them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI is plain text. The problem is that the markup hides the document from a non-specialist reader.

answer.text: A TEI file cannot hold accented letters, so it must be converted before publication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI files are UTF-8 and hold any script. The issue is readability, not character support.

name.text: 02 Question: Content and Presentation Are Two Different Things

questiontext.text: You decide that abbreviations should appear in grey instead of italics. If content and presentation are kept separate, what must you change?

generalfeedback.text: Keep what your document says (the TEI file) separate from how it looks (the display rules), so you can change the look without ever touching the evidence.

answer.text: One display rule; the transcription itself is never touched.

feedback.text: Correct. Keeping the look in display rules means you can improve the presentation without altering the evidence.

answer.text: Every abbreviation in the TEI file, one by one.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would mix presentation into the data. The point of the split is that the file stays fixed.

answer.text: The <teiHeader>, which stores all colour settings for the edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The header records metadata about the document, not how it should be displayed.

answer.text: Nothing; once a TEI file is written, its appearance can never change.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Separating presentation is exactly what lets appearance change freely.

name.text: 03 Question: One File, Many Views

questiontext.text: How can one TEI file produce both a diplomatic view and a reading view?

generalfeedback.text: One encoded file can produce several views; your diplomatic and reading views both come from the <choice> layers you built in Week 6.

answer.text: Each <choice> holds both layers, and each view's rules choose which child of each <choice> to show.

feedback.text: Correct. The Week 6 <orig>/<reg> layers are the raw material; rendering picks one layer per view.

answer.text: The editor keeps two separate transcriptions, one for each view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A single file holds both layers; two files would drift apart.

answer.text: The browser guesses which spelling a reader probably wants.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The choice is made by explicit display rules written by the editor, not by the browser.

answer.text: Only the reading view comes from the file; the diplomatic view is a photograph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both views come from the same encoded file. A diplomatic view is a transcription, not an image.

name.text: 04 Question: The Diplomatic View

questiontext.text: Which reader is best served by the diplomatic view?

generalfeedback.text: The diplomatic view shows the original layer of your file, line by line, for readers who need the document as it actually appears.

answer.text: A historian who wants to see exactly how a clerk in 1791 spelled and abbreviated official titles.

feedback.text: Correct. The diplomatic view keeps original spelling, abbreviations and line breaks for readers who need the document as it appears.

answer.text: A first-year student who wants to read the treaty's terms quickly in modern spelling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That reader needs the reading view, with regularized spelling and expanded abbreviations.

answer.text: A reader who wants a summary of the document instead of its text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neither view summarizes; both present the full text.

answer.text: A reader who wants the editor's commentary on the document's significance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commentary is a separate layer of the edition, not what the diplomatic view provides.

name.text: 05 Question: The Reading View, and What It Hides

questiontext.text: What is the main risk of a smooth reading view?

generalfeedback.text: The reading view makes the document easy to read but hides your interventions; always tell readers what was changed and how to see the original.

answer.text: It hides the editor's interventions so well that readers may think the text is stable and untouched.

feedback.text: Correct. A clean reading text can give a false impression of certainty; tell readers what was changed and how to see the original.

answer.text: It always contains more spelling errors than the diplomatic view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reading view has regularized spelling; its risk is concealment, not errors.

answer.text: It cannot be displayed in a web browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reading views display in any browser.

answer.text: It deletes the original layer from the TEI file permanently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rendering never changes the file; the original layer is simply not shown in this view.

name.text: 06 Question: Who Is Your Reader?

questiontext.text: Why should you name your readers before making any display decision?

generalfeedback.text: Decide who your readers are and what they need to do before you make any display decision; the right look depends on the reader.

answer.text: Because the right look depends on what each reader needs to do: read through, check a word, quote a line, or compare with the image.

feedback.text: Correct. Digital editions can serve different readers with different outputs, but only if you know who they are.

answer.text: Because Moodle requires a reader list before a page can be uploaded.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is an editorial reason, not a platform requirement.

answer.text: Because each reader must be given a separate TEI file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. One file serves all readers; the views differ, not the file.

answer.text: Because naming readers lets you skip the reading view entirely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Knowing your readers usually shows that you need both views.

name.text: 07 Question: Screens, Phones, and Paper

questiontext.text: Which display choice is most likely to fail on a printed page?

generalfeedback.text: Every display decision should survive a phone screen and a printed page, not just your laptop.

answer.text: Explaining a gap only in a hover tooltip.

feedback.text: Correct. Tooltips do not exist on paper, so the gap mark itself must be clear without them.

answer.text: Using a serif font for the reading view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Serif fonts print well; this choice survives every medium.

answer.text: Putting each heading in an <h2> element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Headings print as headings; this is good structure on any device.

answer.text: Showing line numbers in the diplomatic view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line numbers print well and help readers cite precise locations.

name.text: 08 Question: The Rendering Decision Table

questiontext.text: What does each row of the table in RENDERING.md record?

generalfeedback.text: List every element your file uses and decide, in writing, how each one appears in each view; the table in RENDERING.md is today's main deliverable.

answer.text: For one TEI element in your file, how it should appear in the diplomatic view and in the reading view.

feedback.text: Correct. Every row is a decision you can defend, and every row becomes a rule in code.

answer.text: The number of times each element appears in the TEI Guidelines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The table concerns your file and your decisions, not the Guidelines.

answer.text: A list of every spelling you regularized in Week 6.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That list belongs in NORMALIZATION.md; this table records display decisions.

answer.text: The CSS code for each element, written before any decision is made.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Decisions come first, in plain words; code follows them.

name.text: 09 Question: Deciding About Line Breaks

questiontext.text: In the reading view, line breaks disappear. What must you check when that happens?

generalfeedback.text: Decide what each view does with line breaks, and check that removing a break in the reading view never glues two words together or leaves a stray hyphen.

answer.text: That no two words are glued together and no stray hyphen is left inside a word split across lines.

feedback.text: Correct. Whitespace around each <lb/>, and break="no" on split words, decide how the text rejoins.

answer.text: That every line still begins with a capital letter.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lines in the reading view run on; capitalization follows the text, not the old line starts.

answer.text: That the line numbers are still shown in the margin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line numbers belong to the diplomatic view; the reading view usually drops them.

answer.text: That the TEI file has been edited to remove every <lb/>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The file keeps every <lb/>; only the display ignores them.

name.text: 10 Question: Deciding About <choice>: Original and Regularized Spelling

questiontext.text: In Maud Lewis's letter, we was has no <choice> around it. How should it appear?

generalfeedback.text: Show <orig> in the diplomatic view and <reg> in the reading view, decide whether regularized words carry a visible hint, and never let the display change anything the encoding did not.

answer.text: Exactly as written in both views, because the rendering never makes a decision the encoding did not make.

feedback.text: Correct. The Week 6 policy regularized her spelling but not her grammar, and the display must keep that promise.

answer.text: As we were in the reading view, since readers expect standard grammar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would be a silent intervention the encoding never recorded.

answer.text: Hidden in the reading view, since it is non-standard.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hiding her words would drop text from the edition.

answer.text: With [sic] after it in both views.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Her vernacular grammar is not an error and must never be marked as one.

name.text: 11 Question: Deciding About Abbreviations

questiontext.text: What is the worst outcome when displaying expanded abbreviations?

generalfeedback.text: Show abbreviations in the diplomatic view and expansions in the reading view, and choose one consistent way to mark the letters you supplied.

answer.text: Marking supplied letters in some expansions but not in others, so readers cannot tell which letters came from the page.

feedback.text: Correct. Pick one convention, such as italics for <ex>, and use it everywhere.

answer.text: Showing the abbreviation in the diplomatic view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the correct behaviour of the diplomatic view.

answer.text: Putting supplied letters in italics.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Italics is one acceptable convention, as long as it is used consistently.

answer.text: Recording in RENDERING.md that your file does not use <ex>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recording that limit is good practice, not a problem.

name.text: 12 Question: Deciding About Errors and Corrections

questiontext.text: Why does <sic>/<corr> need more care in display than <orig>/<reg>?

generalfeedback.text: Show the error in the diplomatic view and the correction in the reading view, and give readers a visible signal whenever you have corrected the writer.

answer.text: Because it records a judgment that the writer got something wrong, so readers deserve a visible signal that you corrected them.

feedback.text: Correct. A correction is a stronger intervention than a spelling regularization, and should be shown as such.

answer.text: Because browsers cannot display the <corr> element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Browsers display whatever HTML you produce; the issue is editorial, not technical.

answer.text: Because corrections must be hidden from the diplomatic view and the reading view alike.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The diplomatic view shows <sic> and the reading view shows <corr>.

answer.text: Because <sic> is only used for vernacular grammar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Vernacular grammar is not an error and should never carry <sic>.

name.text: 13 Question: Deciding About Uncertainty: <unclear> and <gap/>

questiontext.text: Why should <unclear> text not be marked by colour alone?

generalfeedback.text: Show uncertain readings and gaps in both views, with a mark that does not depend on colour alone.

answer.text: Colour vanishes on a black-and-white printout and some readers cannot distinguish it.

feedback.text: Correct. Use a mark such as a dotted underline, so uncertainty stays visible in every medium.

answer.text: Colour is not allowed in CSS.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CSS supports colour; the problem is relying on it as the only signal.

answer.text: Uncertain readings should be hidden in the reading view anyway.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hiding uncertainty would claim a certainty you do not have; show it in both views.

answer.text: TEI forbids colour attributes on <unclear>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Display rules live in the stylesheet, not in TEI attributes.

name.text: 14 Question: Deciding About Structure: Headings, Paragraphs, Signatures

questiontext.text: Why decide how structural elements such as <head>, <closer> and <pb/> should look, when the answers seem obvious?

generalfeedback.text: Decide how headings, paragraphs, closings and page breaks should look, so that the shape of the original document is visible to the reader.

answer.text: Because an automated tool will make those choices for you unless you have decided first.

feedback.text: Correct. Your decisions become the standard for judging Wednesday's and Friday's tools.

answer.text: Because structural elements are invalid TEI unless they have a display rule.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validity does not depend on display; the decision is editorial.

answer.text: Because browsers refuse to show paragraphs without explicit spacing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Browsers show paragraphs by default; the point is deciding deliberately.

answer.text: Because structural elements are deleted in the reading view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Structure is usually kept in both views so the shape of the document stays visible.

name.text: 15 Question: What HTML Is

questiontext.text: In a minimal HTML page, what does the <head> contain?

generalfeedback.text: HTML is a markup language like TEI, with a <head> for information about the page and a <body> for what the reader sees.

answer.text: Information about the page, such as its character encoding, its title and a link to the stylesheet.

feedback.text: Correct. The <body> holds what the reader sees; the <head> holds information about the page.

answer.text: The first heading of the document, shown in large type.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is <h1>, which goes in the <body>.

answer.text: The full transcription of the document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The transcription goes in the <body>.

answer.text: The TEI header copied unchanged from your XML file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTML's <head> is not the <teiHeader>; it holds page settings.

name.text: 16 Question: HTML Is Forgiving, and That Is Dangerous

questiontext.text: You leave a tag unclosed in your HTML page. What happens?

generalfeedback.text: Browsers silently repair broken HTML, so check your page with a validator rather than trusting how it looks.

answer.text: The browser silently guesses what you meant and shows something anyway, possibly hiding or misplacing text.

feedback.text: Correct. That is why you check the page with a validator rather than trusting how it looks.

answer.text: The browser refuses to open the page and shows an error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is how strict XML tools behave; browsers repair HTML quietly.

answer.text: VS Code automatically deletes the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No tool deletes your file; the danger is a silent repair.

answer.text: Nothing; unclosed tags have no effect in HTML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They can change the structure and appearance of everything after them.

name.text: 17 Question: Mapping TEI Elements to HTML

questiontext.text: How do you carry a TEI <orig> element into hand-written HTML?

generalfeedback.text: Carry each TEI element into HTML as a <span> or <div> whose class repeats the TEI name, using real HTML elements where they exist.

answer.text: As <span class="orig">, keeping the TEI name as the class name.

feedback.text: Correct. Matching class names to TEI names makes the HTML easy to check against the XML.

answer.text: As <orig>, because HTML has the same elements as TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTML has a small fixed set of elements and no <orig>.

answer.text: As <h1>, so that original spellings stand out.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <h1> is a top-level heading and would break the page's structure.

answer.text: By deleting it, since HTML cannot represent original spellings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A <span> with a class can represent any TEI element.

name.text: 18 Question: Line Breaks in HTML

questiontext.text: Why does each <span class="lb"> in the example have a space or new line before it?

generalfeedback.text: Mark each line break with an empty <span class="lb"> carrying its number, and watch the whitespace around it so words neither merge nor split wrongly.

answer.text: So that when the break disappears in the reading view, the words on either side stay apart.

feedback.text: Correct. Whitespace decides whether words merge; split words marked break="no" get no space.

answer.text: Because HTML requires a space before every element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTML has no such rule; the space is there for the reading view.

answer.text: To make the line numbers larger.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Whitespace has no effect on the size of line numbers.

answer.text: So that the validator ignores the span.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validators check every element regardless of spacing.

name.text: 19 Question: What CSS Is

questiontext.text: What does the CSS declaration display: none; do?

generalfeedback.text: CSS is a list of rules, each pairing a selector with declarations; display: none hides an element and display: block puts it on its own line.

answer.text: It hides the selected elements completely, as if they were not on the page.

feedback.text: Correct. This one declaration is enough to hide one layer of every <choice>.

answer.text: It deletes the selected elements from the HTML file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CSS never changes the file; it only controls how it is shown.

answer.text: It puts each selected element on its own line.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is display: block;.

answer.text: It gives the selected elements a dotted underline.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is text-decoration: underline dotted;.

name.text: 20 Question: Two Stylesheets, One Page

questiontext.text: You change the <link> in your page from diplomatic.css to reading.css. What changes?

generalfeedback.text: Put both layers into one HTML page and write two stylesheets that each hide one layer; switching the stylesheet switches the view without touching the text.

answer.text: Only which layer is shown and how the lines flow; the words in the page stay exactly the same.

feedback.text: Correct. Switching the stylesheet switches the view without touching the text.

answer.text: Every <orig> in the HTML is rewritten as a <reg>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both layers stay in the HTML; the stylesheet only hides one of them.

answer.text: The TEI file is regenerated from the HTML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing flows back into the TEI file.

answer.text: The page loses its line numbers permanently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Switching back to the diplomatic stylesheet brings them back.

name.text: 21 Question: Worked Example: A Line of the 1752 Treaty

questiontext.text: After rendering a line by hand, which check matters most?

generalfeedback.text: For each line, check that every element and every word of the TEI appears in the HTML, in order, with correct spacing in both views.

answer.text: That every TEI element and every word appears in the HTML, in order, with correct spacing in both views.

feedback.text: Correct. This line-by-line check is what you repeat for every line you render.

answer.text: That the line looks the same as in a printed edition of the treaty.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your views follow your own decisions, not another edition's layout.

answer.text: That the HTML is shorter than the TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length says nothing about whether text was lost.

answer.text: That the abbreviation has been removed from the HTML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both the abbreviation and the expansion stay in the HTML; the stylesheets choose.

name.text: 22 Question: Worked Example: Maud Lewis's Letter

questiontext.text: How should the reading view of a personal letter differ from its diplomatic view?

generalfeedback.text: A letter's reading view should look like a letter, with its greeting and signature set apart, while its diplomatic view keeps every original line break.

answer.text: The reading view can look like a letter, with greeting and signature set apart, while the diplomatic view keeps every original line break.

feedback.text: Correct. How the writer filled the page is evidence, so the diplomatic view preserves it.

answer.text: The reading view should drop the greeting and signature as unimportant.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dropping text from any view is a fidelity failure.

answer.text: The diplomatic view should correct the writer's grammar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The diplomatic view stays closest to the page; her grammar is never corrected.

answer.text: They should be identical, since a letter has no structure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A letter has a clear structure that both views should respect in their own way.

name.text: 23 Question: Worked Example: The 1791 Decree and French Text

questiontext.text: What does <html lang="fr"> do for the 1791 decree?

generalfeedback.text: Declare <meta charset="utf-8"> and the correct lang on every page, so accented letters display correctly and software knows what language it is reading.

answer.text: It tells browsers, search engines and screen readers that the text is French, so a screen reader pronounces it correctly.

feedback.text: Correct. Declaring the language, together with UTF-8, lets software treat the text properly.

answer.text: It translates the page into French automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The attribute declares the language; it does not translate anything.

answer.text: It makes accented letters display without a character encoding.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accents depend on <meta charset="utf-8">, which you still need.

answer.text: It hides the English introduction from French readers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It hides nothing; mixed-language pages can set lang on individual elements.

name.text: 24 Question: Text That Matters Belongs in the HTML, Not the CSS

questiontext.text: Why should the […] that marks a gap be written into the HTML rather than added by a CSS rule?

generalfeedback.text: Put every editorial mark that carries meaning into the HTML as real text; use CSS only to change how things look.

answer.text: Text added by CSS may not be copied, searched or read aloud, so a reader quoting the page could lose the mark.

feedback.text: Correct. Editorial marks that carry meaning must be real text; CSS is for appearance.

answer.text: CSS cannot add text to a page at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CSS can add text with content, which is exactly why the rule is needed.

answer.text: HTML text always prints in a larger font than CSS text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Font size is not the issue; copying and accessibility are.

answer.text: Validators reject pages that use CSS-generated content.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generated content is valid; it is simply not reliable for meaningful marks.

name.text: 25 Question: Making the Page Readable for Everyone

questiontext.text: Which practice makes your edition more accessible?

generalfeedback.text: Use real headings, strong contrast, more than colour to mark editorial states, and a plain statement at the top of each view saying what the reader is seeing.

answer.text: Using real headings in order, strong contrast, more than colour to mark editorial states, and a plain statement of what each view shows.

feedback.text: Correct. These cost little when built in from the start and help every reader.

answer.text: Using light grey text on a white page for elegance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Low contrast makes text hard to read for many people.

answer.text: Marking unclear readings in red only.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Colour alone is invisible to some readers and to black-and-white printers.

answer.text: Making headings with bold paragraphs instead of heading elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Screen-reader users navigate by real heading elements.

name.text: 26 Question: Checking That Nothing Was Lost

questiontext.text: Which of these is one of the three fidelity checks for your hand-made rendering?

generalfeedback.text: Check your rendering against both the image and the TEI file, word by word and line by line, and record every problem you find and fix.

answer.text: Counting the words in ten lines of the TEI and in each view, and explaining any difference.

feedback.text: Correct. Together with two read-backs, against the image and the TEI file, the count catches dropped words.

answer.text: Asking a friend whether the page looks attractive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Appearance is not fidelity; the checks compare words and lines.

answer.text: Running a spell checker on the reading view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A spell checker cannot tell whether text was dropped, and would flag legitimate original spellings.

answer.text: Checking that the page loads in under one second.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed has nothing to do with whether the rendering preserves the text.

name.text: 27 Question: Why Do This by Hand?

questiontext.text: Why build the page by hand before using XSLT on Wednesday?

generalfeedback.text: Your hand-made page is the ground truth for this week; without it, you cannot tell whether Wednesday's and Friday's automatic renderings are right.

answer.text: Because the hand-made page is the ground truth against which the automatic and AI renderings are measured.

feedback.text: Correct. You can only judge a tool's decisions after you have made your own.

answer.text: Because XSLT cannot transform XML into HTML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transforming XML into HTML is exactly what XSLT is for.

answer.text: Because the hand-made page will replace the TEI file as the master copy.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The TEI file remains the master; the page is one rendering of it.

answer.text: Because automatic renderings are never used in real editing projects.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Real projects test their encodings with XSLT stylesheets routinely.

name.text: 28 Question: Hypothetical Scenario: The Quotation That Went Wrong

questiontext.text: In the scenario, the edition's encoding was flawless. What misled the student?

generalfeedback.text: A perfect encoding can still mislead readers if the rendering hides its interventions; a rendering statement and a link to the diplomatic view prevent it.

answer.text: The rendering regularized every word without any statement, hint or link to the diplomatic view.

feedback.text: Correct. A perfect encoding can still mislead if the rendering hides its interventions.

answer.text: The TEI file was missing every <orig> element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The scenario says the encoding had every <orig> and <reg> in place.

answer.text: The photograph of the original was mislabelled.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The photograph is how the professor caught the problem.

answer.text: Regularization is never acceptable in a reading view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regularizing was reasonable; hiding it was the failure.

name.text: 29 Question: Saving Your Work in Git

questiontext.text: In what order should you commit your Step 1 work?

generalfeedback.text: Keep RENDERING.md, your HTML page and both stylesheets in your repository, and commit your decisions before your code.

answer.text: RENDERING.md first, once your decisions are written, then the HTML and each stylesheet separately once they work.

feedback.text: Correct. Small commits in that order show that you decided first and coded second.

answer.text: Everything in one commit at the end of the week.

feedback.text: Incorrect. One large commit hides the order of your work and makes mistakes hard to undo.

answer.text: The stylesheets first, then the decisions that justify them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Decisions come before code.

answer.text: Only the HTML; decision files do not belong in the repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RENDERING.md is part of your edition and belongs in the repository.

name.text: 30 Question: Review and Step 1 Checklist

questiontext.text: Which pair of items is required for Step 1 of the rendering week?

generalfeedback.text: Completing Step 1 gives you a written set of display decisions and a hand-made page that carries them out, the standard against which every automatic rendering this week will be judged.

answer.text: A complete decision table in RENDERING.md and a hand-made HTML page with diplomatic and reading stylesheets.

feedback.text: Correct. Together they are the standard against which every automatic rendering this week is judged.

answer.text: An XSLT stylesheet and a CETEIcean page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are Wednesday's work; Step 1 is manual.

answer.text: An AI-generated stylesheet and its audit report.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is Friday's work.

answer.text: A printed PDF of the edition and a new TEI schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Print stylesheets come on Wednesday, and no new schema is needed.
